name: Choice Under Tradeoffs
big_picture: The course begins before strategic conflict: a person has to be able to rank outcomes before a model can ask what they will choose. This theme is about turning vague wants into a disciplined object that can survive calculation without pretending the number is literal happiness.
why_this_theme_matters: Without this layer, every later game table is decoration. Payoffs, expected payoffs, bidding values, outside options, and bargaining surplus all assume that the model has already said what each participant is trying to protect or gain.
cross_course_argument: The first lectures use preferences and utility to build the measuring stick used everywhere else. Later lectures quietly reuse the same stick in mixed strategies, Bayesian games, auctions, and bargaining: once risk, hidden values, or future rounds enter, the course still needs a way to compare alternatives before the player knows which world will arrive.
mathematical_spine: The spine is preference turned into a utility number, then utility averaged over uncertainty when probabilities matter. The primitive is not arithmetic for its own sake; it is a way to preserve the order of choices while allowing the course to compute best responses and expected gains.
where_analogy_breaks: The analogy breaks if the utility number is read as a psychological meter. In these lectures, utility is a representation of choice behavior. Changing the units can leave ordinal choice unchanged, while expected-utility comparisons need stronger structure because lotteries require meaningful tradeoffs across uncertain outcomes.
lecture_evidence_chain: The opening preference and utility evidence anchors the construction of rankings and numerical payoffs. The expected-utility evidence then shows why probabilities must be folded into payoff comparisons when the outcome is uncertain. Those records support the theme directly; later uses in auctions and Bayesian games are cross-theme synthesis.

name: Strategic Dependence
big_picture: This is the point where ordinary decision-making becomes game theory. A move can be sensible or foolish only after the other players choices are included, so the course needs representations that keep everyone’s actions in the same picture.
why_this_theme_matters: Strategic dependence is the reason a payoff matrix, a game tree, dominance, deletion, and rationalizability exist. They are all ways to avoid judging an action in isolation when its consequence is created jointly with other actions.
cross_course_argument: The strategic-form lecture makes dependence visible in a table. The extensive-form lecture shows that timing can be part of the dependence. Dominance and iterated deletion then ask whether some actions can be removed before equilibrium reasoning begins, while rationalizability asks what choices can still make sense under some belief about others.
mathematical_spine: The spine is a payoff map from action profiles to player-specific payoffs, plus pruning rules that compare one action against another across possible opponent actions. The math matters because it forces the analyst to say exactly which opponent moves make a strategy look good or bad.
where_analogy_breaks: A table can hide timing and information, while a tree can become misleading if the information sets or payoffs are wrong. Dominance is also fragile: strict dominance is a strong deletion rule, but weak dominance and belief-based arguments require more care.
lecture_evidence_chain: The strategic-form and extensive-form records supply the representation evidence. Dominance, iterated deletion, and rationalizability records support the pruning and belief-based parts of the theme. The theme argument is the bridge between those lecture spans.

name: Equilibrium As Mutual Consistency
big_picture: Equilibrium reasoning asks for a prediction that does not immediately fall apart when each player looks at their own incentives. It is less a claim that the outcome is good than a consistency check on everyone’s planned behavior.
why_this_theme_matters: Many stories about strategic behavior sound plausible until one player can profitably change. Nash equilibrium, mixed strategies, zero-sum value, and minimax reasoning give the course tests for whether a proposed outcome survives individual deviation.
cross_course_argument: Best response supplies the one-player test. Nash makes all players pass that test at once. Mixed strategies show that stability may require deliberate randomness. Zero-sum and minimax sharpen the same idea under pure conflict, where protecting yourself against the opponent’s best attack becomes the prediction logic.
mathematical_spine: The spine is the best-response correspondence and the fixed point idea behind mutual consistency. In zero-sum settings the same pressure becomes maximin/minimax reasoning: choose a plan whose worst consequence is as strong as possible because the opponent’s gain is your loss.
where_analogy_breaks: Equilibrium does not mean efficient, ethical, or likely in a behavioral sense. It also changes shape when time, private information, or beliefs enter; that is why later lectures need subgame-perfect, Bayesian Nash, and perfect Bayesian equilibrium rather than one universal test.
lecture_evidence_chain: Best-response and Nash records anchor the general stability test. Mixed-strategy records support intentional randomization. Zero-sum and minimax records support the special case where conflict turns stability into security-level reasoning.

name: Time, Threats, And Credibility
big_picture: When actions unfold over time, a plan is not credible merely because someone announces it early. The course’s time-based concepts ask whether a later action will still be worth taking when the later moment actually arrives.
why_this_theme_matters: Threats, promises, offers, refusals, and continuation plans are common in real strategic settings. Without a credibility test, a model may predict behavior based on statements that no rational player would carry out later.
cross_course_argument: Game trees represent timing. Backward induction solves from the end because the end constrains the beginning. Subgame perfection removes noncredible threats. One-shot deviation gives a local test for dynamic optimality. Bargaining uses the same time pressure when delay changes the value of agreement.
mathematical_spine: The spine is recursive value: assign values to later decision nodes, then bring those values backward to earlier choices. Discounting enters when waiting changes payoffs. The math is important because the future is not a slogan; it is a continuation value that changes current incentives.
where_analogy_breaks: Backward logic can overstate precision if the tree omits uncertainty, private information, renegotiation, or limited foresight. A threat that is credible in one subgame may fail once beliefs or outside options change.
lecture_evidence_chain: Extensive-form evidence anchors trees and histories. Backward-induction, subgame-perfection, one-shot-deviation, and bargaining evidence records provide the credibility checks that make this theme more than a timing label.

name: Repeated Interaction And Cooperation
big_picture: Repeated interaction changes the meaning of a current move because today’s gain can affect tomorrow’s treatment. The theme asks when the future is strong enough to discipline short-run temptation.
why_this_theme_matters: Many relationships, markets, and organizations do not happen once. Cooperation, punishment, reputation, and tacit collusion become possible only when players expect their current action to be remembered or answered later.
cross_course_argument: Finite repetition shows the known-last-round problem: if nothing follows the final period, cooperation can unravel backward. Infinite repetition removes the fixed endpoint and lets trigger strategies work. The folk theorem shows how large the set of sustainable outcomes can become, while cartel applications translate the abstract logic into market behavior.
mathematical_spine: The spine is discounted continuation value. A player compares the one-time gain from cheating with the discounted stream lost after punishment. The inequality matters because cooperation is sustained only when future losses outweigh present temptation.
where_analogy_breaks: The repeated-game analogy breaks when monitoring is poor, players are too impatient, punishment is not credible, entry changes the player set, or the horizon is known to end. Future discipline is a mechanism with conditions, not a guarantee of cooperation.
lecture_evidence_chain: Finite and infinite repeated-game records support the horizon contrast. Folk theorem evidence supports the broad sustainability result. Cartel evidence supplies the applied interpretation in pricing and market competition.

name: Private Information And Beliefs
big_picture: Strategic choices often happen when one person knows something another person does not: a value, cost, type, signal, or history. This theme is about making hidden information explicit enough to reason about.
why_this_theme_matters: If private information is ignored, the model treats different kinds of players as if they were the same. Bayesian games, types, beliefs, Bayesian Nash equilibrium, and perfect Bayesian equilibrium are tools for keeping those hidden differences inside the analysis.
cross_course_argument: Types and beliefs give names to unknown facts and probability stories. Bayesian Nash asks each type to choose optimally before all hidden information is revealed. Perfect Bayesian equilibrium adds time and updating, requiring beliefs and future actions to fit the observed path.
mathematical_spine: The spine is expected payoff over types or histories. A player chooses a strategy after averaging over what might be true, weighted by beliefs. Bayes rule becomes important when observed actions should change those beliefs.
where_analogy_breaks: Beliefs are not free excuses. Off-path beliefs, impossible observations, and strategic signaling can make the model delicate. Treating any arbitrary belief as equally disciplined can make a private-information model explain too much.
lecture_evidence_chain: Bayesian-game and type evidence records support the representation of hidden information. Bayesian Nash records support type-contingent best response. PBE records support the dynamic link between beliefs, observed behavior, and sequential rationality.

name: Mechanisms, Auctions, And Markets
big_picture: Mechanism lectures reverse the usual question. Instead of only predicting behavior under fixed rules, they ask how rules should be built when participants will respond strategically to those rules.
why_this_theme_matters: Auctions, online ads, and market institutions are engineered strategic environments. A rule that looks good mechanically can fail if bidders shade bids, hide values, exploit ranking formulas, or change behavior once the rule is known.
cross_course_argument: Auction lectures show how bidding rules translate private values into allocations and payments. Revenue equivalence shows that different rules can agree under strong assumptions. Ad auctions add platform constraints such as clicks, positions, and quality scores. Cartel material shows the darker side: firms may also design informal punishment rules for themselves.
mathematical_spine: The spine is incentive compatibility joined to payoff mapping. The designer writes a rule, then checks whether each participant’s best response under that rule produces the intended allocation, payment, or information revelation.
where_analogy_breaks: Auction results can collapse when assumptions change: correlated values, risk aversion, budgets, entry costs, reserve prices, quality scores, or repeated interaction can all move the answer. Design claims have to travel with their assumptions.
lecture_evidence_chain: Auction, revenue-equivalence, and ad-auction records support the formal market-design side. Cartel evidence links rules and incentives to repeated market behavior rather than centralized design.

name: Communication And Knowledge
big_picture: Communication changes games only when it changes what people believe others know or intend. This theme separates empty words from messages and public facts that can actually coordinate behavior.
why_this_theme_matters: Real strategic life is full of announcements, signals, advice, disclosures, threats, and public information. The course needs tools for asking when these things persuade, reveal, mislead, or coordinate.
cross_course_argument: Signaling studies costly or informative actions by privately informed senders. Cheap talk asks when costless words can still matter. Common knowledge pushes beyond private awareness into higher-order awareness: not just knowing a fact, but knowing that others know it too.
mathematical_spine: The spine is belief updating plus incentive compatibility, with knowledge recursion for public coordination. A message matters only if the receiver’s belief changes and the sender had the right incentive to send that message in the first place.
where_analogy_breaks: A signal is not the same as cheap talk, and mutual knowledge is not automatically common knowledge. Costs, preferences, observability, and higher-order beliefs determine which communication model applies.
lecture_evidence_chain: Signaling and cheap-talk evidence records support the incentive side of communication. Common-knowledge records support the higher-order knowledge side, where public facts become strategic only through shared awareness.
